LESSON 2 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Cybersecurity vs Information Security

Information security protects information; cyber security protects the machines that carry it. One employee file, in three places, shows why the difference changes the plan.

Beginner3 min
Why this matters

"Cyber security" and "information security" are used as if they were the same thing. They are not, and the difference tells you what a plan has to cover.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • define information security and cyber security without using each other's words
  • classify a given risk as information, cyber, or both
  • explain why a plan that only covers computers is incomplete

In plain English

Information security protects information wherever it is: on paper, in a conversation, on a whiteboard, in someone's head. Cyber security protects the computers and networks that carry information.

Every cyber security problem is also an information security problem, because computers hold information. But not every information security problem is a cyber problem. A salary sheet left on a printer is an information security problem with nothing cyber about it.

How it works

The two fields ask the same three things — is it available, is it correct, is it private — but they answer with different tools.

  • Information security answers with cabinets, lockable rooms, clear rules about who may speak to whom, and paper trails.
  • Cyber security answers with encryption, access control, logging, network boundaries and patching.
  • Both answer to the same management question: what are we protecting, and who is allowed to touch it?

That is why a serious security programme is not run by a single team. The person who controls physical keys and the person who controls cloud permissions are protecting the same asset from two directions.

A worked example

One employee file, in three different places. Same information, different discipline:

  • A paper file in a locked cabinet, in an office with a door code. Information security only. Nobody needs a firewall to protect it.
  • The same file on a shared drive, readable by everyone in the company. Both. The rule about who may read it is information security; the permissions that enforce it are cyber security.
  • The same file in an email attachment sent to a personal address. Both, and now the cyber failure — it left the boundary — decided the information outcome.

In practice the third one is how most real incidents start: not a clever attacker, just information leaving a boundary that nobody was watching.

The mistake most beginners make

Treating the words as interchangeable, then building a plan that only covers computers. Such a plan has nothing to say about a printed sheet left in a meeting room, a phone call to the wrong person, or a laptop screen on a train.

The reverse mistake is just as common in small organisations: "we don't have cyber security" — said while holding a phone that has email, a customer list and a payment app on it.

Try it in two minutes

Pick three pieces of information you handled this week. For each, write where it lives and who can reach it:

  • Where does it physically or digitally sit right now?
  • Who could read it without asking you?
  • Would you find out if they did?

Anything that lives on a computer is now in cyber territory. Anything that does not is still information security, and still your problem.

Practice / apply

No tools needed. Take three pieces of information you handle in a normal week and write down where each one physically lives.

Key takeaways

  • Information security protects information; cyber security protects the machines that carry it.
  • All cyber problems are information problems; not all information problems are cyber.
  • A plan that only covers computers leaves out paper, speech and screens.
  • Most incidents start with information crossing a boundary nobody was watching.
